Review session MT1 (20 September 2023)

Reynolds transport theorem

DtDΨ​=accumulationdtd​(∭ρψdV)​​+efflux (in - out)∬ρψ(v​⋅n^)dA​​;ψ=dmdΨ​(intensive;Ψ extensive);Ψ={m,P​,E}

(D/Dt = material derivative.)

Mass balance (continuity equation): Ψ = m; ψ=dmdm​=1:

DtDm​​=rate of accumulation of mass w/n CV (@ SS = 0)dtd​(∭CV​ρdV)​​+net outward flow of mass across the CS, "efflux"∬CS​ρ(v​⋅n^)dA​​

Efflux > 0 (net mass going out); < 0 (net mass going in); = 0 (mass w/n CV is constant) ↓ evaluate at all control surfaces of the chosen control volume. For incompressible flow ρ = constant ∴ for SS, incompressible flow through a CV: ∬CS​ρ(v​⋅n^)dA=dtdm​​=0.

(figure: a tank with inlet ① (A1​, v1​, inward-pointing normal) and outlet ② (A2​, v2​).) @ SS, incompressible:

ρ∬A1​​(v​⋅n^)dA+ρ∬A2​​(v​⋅n^)dA=0⇒ρ(−v1​)∬A1​​dA+ρv2​∬A2​​dA=0⇒ρv1​A1​=ρv2​A2​​

↑ Irrespective of the flow inside the control volume! (Would work anytime for constant velocity!)

Momentum balance: Ψ=mv​; ψ=dmd(mv​)​=v​dmdm​​+mdmdv​​​=v​. RTT becomes:

DtD(mv​)​=dtd​(∭CV​ρv​dV)+∬CS​ρv​(v​⋅n^)dA;Newton’s second law: ∑F​=DtD(mv​)​ ∴sum of forces acting on CV, i.e. on the fluid∑F​​​=rate of acc. of momentum w/n CVdtd​(∭CV​ρv​dV)​​+net rate of momentum efflux from CV∬CS​ρv​(v​⋅n^)dA​​

@ SS, Cartesian coord.: ∑Fx​=∬ρvx​(v​⋅n^)dA; ∑Fy​=∬ρvy​(v​⋅n^)dA; ∑Fz​=∬ρvz​(v​⋅n^)dA.

Find the force exerted on a pipe bend resulting from steady state, incompressible flow as shown. W represents gravitational force.

(figure: flow enters horizontally at ① and leaves at ② angled down at θ; W acts downward; pressures act on both faces.)

① Define CV → all fluid in the pipe. There are external forces acting on this fluid (pressure; τw​) } total resultant force is defined F​.

Force balance: (sketch: n^1​=−e^x​ at the inlet, n^2​ at the outlet; v​2​=ae^x​+b(e^y​) with cosθ=v2​a​, sinθ=v2​b​, so v​2​=v2​cosθe^x​−v2​sinθe^y​.)

SurfaceMomentum balance
①∑F1​=∬A1​​ρv​(v​⋅n^)dA1​=ρv12​e^x​∬A1​​(v1​e^x​⋅(−e^x​))dA1​=(−ρv12​A1​)e^x​
③ (walls)∑F3​=∬A3​​ρv​(v​⋅n^)​dA3​=0
②∑F2​=ρv​(v2​)∬dA2​=ρv2​A2​(v2​cosθ−v2​sinθ​)=(ρv22​A2​cosθ)e^x​−(ρv22​A2​sinθ)e^y​
∴∑F​=∑F1​+∑F2​→total force acting on the fluid in the CV:∑F​=(−ρv12​A1​+ρv22​A2​cosθ−ρv22​A2​sinθ​)xy​

Since the entire system is stationary → net forces are zero: F​ext​−∑F​=0. Taking the control volume as the entire object:

Fextx​=P1​A1​−P2​A2​cosθ+Bx​(resultant force on the fluid; don’t know the sign);Fexty​=−W+P2​A2​sinθ+By​ (P1​A1​−P2​A2​cosθ+Bx​−(−ρv12​A1​+ρv22​A2​cosθ)−W+P2​A2​sinθ+By​−(−ρv22​A2​sinθ)​)xy​=0→solve for Bx​,By​

Now the force exerted on the pipe by the fluid will be equal and opposite to the force exerted by the pipe on the fluid.

OH review question (23 October 2023)

Problem 6.47 — two-layer flow down an incline. Two different fluids with different densities (ρ₁, ρ₂) and viscosities (μ₁, μ₂) are layered on a long plate tilted at an angle β to the horizontal. The thickness of the bottom and more dense fluid is h₁; the thickness of the top and less dense fluid is h₂. The bottom plate is stationary, and a flow is produced by gravity. The flow is steady and both fluids are incompressible. Solve for the velocity profile in a Cartesian coordinate system with flow in the x-direction; y is the direction perpendicular to the plates, with y = 0 at the surface of the bottom plate. (The Cartesian Navier–Stokes equations E-1 to E-3 are pasted below it.)

Steady, incompressible. If pressure does not cancel (multiple coordinate dependence):

∂y∂P​=α⇒P=αy+f(x);∂x∂P​=dxdf​;BC: @ y=h,P=Patm​⇒Patm​=αh+f(x)⇒f(x)=β=constant⇒dxdf​=0⇒dxdP​=0

Review session exam 2 (27 October 2023)

Algorithm:

  1. Sketch the problem (if no figure provided) — + choose coordinate system (or check consistency w/ one provided); + clearly understand where flow is, where the boundaries are.
  2. Characterize the flow: v​=( ); g​=( ) — + Newtonian? Incompressible? Steady state? Where is bulk fluid flowing? + Is it open to environment? → most likely no pressure gradients! + Is it inclined? How is gravity affected?
  3. Continuity equation — + simplify (and write!) the modified equation (after cancellations); + clearly write why you are cancelling out terms.
  4. Equation of motion (microscopic momentum balance) — + incompressible, Newtonian (constant viscosity) → Navier–Stokes; + non-Newtonian → Cauchy momentum balance.
  5. Boundary conditions (BCs) — + no. of BCs corresponds to the order of the differential equation; + @ solid surfaces → no slip; @ interfaces → shear stress.
  6. Solve for velocity profile (and/or pressure field) — + integration → keep check of constants; + solve for constants at the very end; + if pressure is imp. (i.e. flow in a closed pipe) → then need additional BCs for this.
  7. Evaluate Q, F​ given the solved velocity profile.

Exam-taking strategies: (1) Don’t panic! — read the question carefully; understand where, what, how; check the coordinate system!! (2) Maximize points — focus on questions w/ higher points (more points ~ more time); attempt everything & write a best guess if short of time (partial credits).

Practice 1 — falling fluid between two plates

An incompressible fluid confined between two parallel, vertical surfaces. One surface is stationary, whereas the other is moving upward at a constant velocity v0. If we consider the fluid Newtonian and the flow laminar: sketch the velocity streamlines and find the velocity profile in this flow.

(figure: fluid between a stationary wall at x = 0 and a wall at x = L moving up at v0​; y up.)

    • Cartesian coordinate system (xyz); + gravity ✓; + Newtonian, incomp. ✓; + pressure? → closed system so most likely present.
  • v​=(0,−vy​,0)xyz​ [?]; vy​=f(x) (wide/infinite wall, i.e. symmetric in z direction); g​=(0,−g,0)xyz​

→ Mass balance: 0=∇⋅v​ (SS, incomp.): ∂x∂vx​​​+∂y∂vy​​+∂z∂vz​​​=0 ∴ ∂y∂vy​​=0 [developed flow].

→ EOM: ρ(∂t∂v​​​+v​⋅∇v​)=−∇p+μ∇2v​+ρg​:

  • x: 0=−∂x∂p​
  • y: 0=−∂y∂p​+μ(∂x2∂2vy​​)+ρgy​; gy​=−g
  • z: 0=−∂z∂p​

No pressure gradients in x & z direction; P = f(y); ∂y∂P​=dydP​ = constant:

∴not a function of x!=λμ1​(dydP​−ρg)​​=∂x2∂2vy​​⇒∂x∂vy​​=μλ​x+c1​⇒vy​=μλ​2x2​+c1​x+c2​

BCs: @ x = 0, vy​=0 → c2​=0; @ x = L, vy​=v0​ → (v0​−μλ​2L2​)L1​=c1​, c1​=Lv0​​−2μλL​:

vy​=μλ​2x2​+(Lv0​​−2μλL​)x​Sketch it out!

Transcriber’s note: λ is defined with 1/μ already included, so μλ​ in the integration double-counts μ; as written.

Practice 2 — Problems 6.44 & 6.52: upward pressure-driven flow in a tube, non-Newtonian fluid (power law); incompressible; SS

Problem 6.44: calculate the velocity profile and flow rate for pressure-driven flow of an incompressible, Newtonian liquid in a vertical pipe of radius R. The pressure at the bottom entrance to the tube is P₀; at a point a distance L upward the pressure is P_L. Assume that the flow is well developed and at steady state. Do not neglect gravity. Problem 6.52: repeat problem 6.44 with a power-law, generalized Newtonian fluid with parameters m and n.

(sketch: a vertical tube of radius R from z = 0 (P=P0​) to z = L (P=PL​).) v​=(0,0,vz​)rθz​; g​=(0,0,−g)rθz​; flow profile? pressure profile? cylindrical coordinates.

→ Mass balance: ∇⋅v​=0 (incomp., SS): ∂t∂ρ​​+r1​∂r∂​(ρrvr​​)+r1​∂θ∂​(ρvθ​​)+∂z∂​(ρvz​)=0 ⇒ ∂z∂vz​​=0.

→ Non-Newtonian flow → cannot use Navier–Stokes! (only incompressible flow) — Table B.6: cylindrical coordinates of the Cauchy momentum balance. τ​​=η(γ˙​)γ˙​​​ (μ for Newtonian); γ˙​​​=(∇v​+(∇v​)T); η(γ˙​)=mγ˙​n−1. Equation B.8-2 (Newtonian constitutive equation) gives the components of γ˙​​​; only τrz​=∂r∂vz​​ (times η) survives:

γ˙​=∥γ˙​​​∥=​​00∂r∂vz​​​000​∂r∂vz​​00​​​=21​(sum of squares of each term in γ˙​​​)​=21​[(∂r∂vz​​)2+(∂r∂vz​​)2]​=​∂r∂vz​​​

As r↑, vz​↓ (closer to the wall): ∂r∂vz​​<0→−∂r∂vz​​>0 ∴ γ˙​=−∂r∂vz​​.

τ​​=mγ˙​n−1γ˙​​​=m(−∂r∂vz​​)n−1​00⋅​000​∂vz​/∂r00​​∴τrz​=m(−∂r∂vz​​)n−1(∂r∂vz​​)=f(θ,z)

Only τrz​ exists (due to flow direction), which is a function of r (and not z!):

  • r-direction: 0=−∂r∂P​; θ-direction: 0=−r1​∂θ∂P​ } P has no θ & r dependence: −∂z∂P​=−dzdP​
  • z-direction: 0=−∂z∂P​+(r1​∂r∂​(rτrz​))+−ρgρgz​​​
∴=f(r)dzdP​+ρg​​==f(z)r1​drd​(rτrz​)​​=λ→solve them separately!
  • dzdP​+ρg=λ ⇒ P=(λ−ρg)z+c1​; @ z = 0, P = P₀ → c1​=P0​; @ z = L, P = P_L → (PL​−P0​)=(λ−ρg)L ⇒ λ=LPL​−P0​​+ρg
  • drd​(rτrz​)=λr ⇒ τrz​=2λr​+rc1​​; @ r = 0, ∂r∂vz​​=0, τrz​=0 } c1​=0 ⇒ τrz​=2λr​
  • With τrz​=m(−∂r∂vz​​)n−1(∂r∂vz​​)⋅(−1)(−1)​=−m(−∂r∂vz​​)n: 2λr​=−m(−∂r∂vz​​)n ⇒ −drdvz​​=(2m−λ​)1/nr1/n ⇒ vz​=−(2m−λ​)1/n(n1​+1)r1/n+1​+c1​
  • @ r = R, vz​=0 } c1​=(−2mλ​)1/n(n1​+1)R(1/n+1)​
∴vz​=(−2mλ​)1/n(n1​+1)1​(Rn1​+1−rn1​+1)​

Boundary layer

  • Laminar [Rex​<2×105]: + no-slip condition (gives rise to flow dependent on two directions). (sketch: smooth flat-plate BL of thickness δ growing from the leading edge over a plate of length L and width W.)
δ=(ρv∞​25μ​)l​=Re​5x​​(l=distance from leading edge of the plate, not a var!);F​=∬S​[n^⋅Π​​]@surf​dSpg 693​τ~w​=0.332μv∞​(μlρv∞​​)1/2​ ★Fdrag​=∫0W​∫0L​τ~w​dx1​dx3​;Re=μρv∞​l​;CD​=21​ρv∞2​WLFdrag​​=(Re)L1/2​1.328​
  • Turbulent [Rex​>1×106]: + downstream flow (from the leading edge) the velocity becomes unstable } i.e. only starts after an initial laminar-regime BL; + thicker layers (that have different x1​ dependence) } higher drag on the flat plate. (sketch: laminar BL up to a certain x1​, then turbulent.)
δ=(Re)l1/7​0.16l​;CD​=(ReL​)1/70.031​;Cf​=(Rex​)1/70.027​=ρU02​2τw​​;U0​=v∞​;τw​=(Rex​)1/70.0135ρv∞2​​​

General relationship: CD​=(KE)(Area)Fdrag​​=(KE)(Area)∬τw​dA​=(KE)(Area)∬Cf​⋅(2ρv∞2​​)dA​ (Cf​ dependent on lam/turb and on the x var) } use Cf​ (unless evaluating for the entire plate BL!).

1. Come sail away

You are captain on a sailboat. Your boat is moving completely due to the force of the wind in the sail. The wind enters the sail region through an area that is roughly 5 m², with a velocity v​1​=(v1​,0,0)ijk​. The wind leaves the sail region through an area that is also 5 m², with a velocity v​2​=(v2i​,v2j​,0)ijk​. Your boat is 30 m long, and it can be modeled as a 2-sided flat plate. You can consider that the boat extends 2 m below the surface of the water. On this day, your boat is moving at a constant velocity of 0.5 m/s. The water has a density of 1000 kg/m³ and a viscosity of 9×10⁻³ poise. The viscosity of air is 1.7×10⁻⁵ poise, and the density of air is 1.2 kg/m³. (figure: the sail at θ = 40° deflecting the wind from A1​=5 m² to A2​=5 m² (assume no friction); boat 30 m long.)

[Boat] two-sided flat plate (sketches: side view of the boat — the submerged hull 30 m long and 2 m deep, “kinda like a hydrofoil of a sailboat”; 1 poise = 0.1 kg/m·s).

Water BL:

ReL​=μρv∞​L​=(0.9)×10−3(1000)(0.5)(30)​=1.67×107(turbulent);transition: 1×106=(0.9×10−3)(1000)(0.5)(L)​⇒L=1.8 m

(sketch: laminar BL to x = 1.8 m, turbulent after.) τwl​=(Rex​)1/20.332ρv∞2​​; τwt​=(Rex​)1/70.0135ρv∞2​​:

FD​=∬τwl​dxdy+∬τwt​dxdy=∫02​∫01.8​(μρv∞​x​)1/2(0.332)ρv∞2​​dxdy+∫02​∫1.830​(μρv∞​x​)1/70.0135ρv∞2​​dxdy =2(0.332)ρμ​(v∞​)3/2(1/2)x1/2​​01.8​+2(0.0135)ρ6/7v∞13/7​μ1/7(6/7)x6/7​​1.830​ FD​=[2(0.332)(1000)(0.9×10−3)​(0.5)3/2(1/2)(1.81/2)​]+[2(0.0135)(1000)6/7(0.5)13/7(0.9×10−3)1/7(6/7)306/7−(1.8)6/7​]=0.5976+19.99

FD​=20.6 N (force of drag from just 1 BL); total FD​ (from both BL) ⇒ 2FD​=FDtotal​ ⇒ FDtotal​=41.2 N​.

Evaluate the velocities using momentum balance (β = 1, turbulent):

dtdP​​​+∑ρcosθi​Ai​⟨vi​⟩2v^i​=∑f​=negligiblef​g​+f​in​+f​out​​​+f​w​;f​w​=−FDtotal​ ρcosθ1​A1​⟨v1​⟩2v^1​+ρcosθ2​A2​⟨v2​⟩2v^2​=−41.2 N⇒ρA[(−1)⟨v1​⟩2e^x​+(1)⟨v2​⟩2(cos50sin50​)]=−41.2 N

Only care about the i-th direction: ρA[−⟨v1​⟩2+⟨v2​⟩2cos50]=−41.2; finding the relative velocity (since the boat is moving as well), v1​=v2​=(v1​−0.5):

ρA[−(v1​−0.5)2+(v1​−0.5)2cos50]=−41.2⇒(v1​−0.5)2ρA(−1+cos(50))=−41.2⇒v1​=4.88 m/s​

Raise the roof

(figure: wind v∞​ blowing over a house with a 15 m × 15 m roof; a board 1 m from the edge and 3 m from the bottom, 10 m long; ”e^z​ comes out of the page”. In red: the board region from x = 1 to 5 m and y = 3 to 13.5 m.)

Given an FD,fixer​ [?]: FD​=Cf​⋅Fg​; Fg​=m⋅g. We don’t know v∞​ → have to assume a regime since we cannot find Re. Assuming turbulent on the board (i.e. the laminar regime has been crossed before the board ↓ but we don’t care):

The boundary layer is developing in the y direction → that is the characteristic dimension now (given the coordinate system we have). FD​=∫313.5​∫15​0.0135ρ6/7v∞13/7​μ1/7(y)−1/7dxdy=(5)0.0135ρ6/7v∞13/7​μ1/7(6/7)(y)6/7​​313.5​ Cf​⋅(Fg​)=v∞13/7​[(5)(0.0135)(1.3)6/7(1.7×10−5)1/76/7(13.56/7−36/7)​]⇒(1.2)(70)=v∞13/7​(0.1385)⇒v∞​=(0.1385(1.2)(70)​)7/13 v∞​=31.5≈32 m/s​;assumption check @ start of board: Re=(1.7×10−5)(1.3)(31.5)(3)​>1×106✓board is in turbulent

δturb=(Rex​)1/70.16x​ → x @ which we want to measure the thickness (δ changes w/ x!). ∴ @ x = 14.5 (the bird’s nest):

δturb=(μρv∞​(14.5)​)1/7(0.16)(14.5)​=[(1.7×10−5)(1.3)(31.5)(14.5)​]1/7(0.16)(14.5)​=0.194 m

Final exam review session (5 December 2023)

Turbulence → time-averaged quantity: quantity​=∫t0​t1​​quantity⋅dt [?] ✓ steady state ✓.

Question 1

A liquid with a given viscosity (mew) enters and leaves the above bend as shown. Solve the following questions. (figure: a bend with inlet a (radius Ra​, flow up, v​a​=⟨v⟩a​e^y​, normal n^a​ down) and outlet b (radius Rb​, flow out down-left at 18° from vertical, v​b​=⟨v⟩b​e^vb​​, normal n^b​).)

(a) Using Reynolds transport theorem, solve for the overall force on the fluid.

RTT:dtdP​​+∬CS​ρ(v​⋅n^)v​dS=on CV∑​F​

Taking the fluid inside the pipe as the CV: there is flow through surface A and surface B.

Inlet: v​a​=(0,⟨v⟩,0)xyz​; n^a​=−e^y​=(0,−1,0)xyz​:

∬inlet​ρv​a​(n^⋅v​a​)dS=∫02π​∫0Ra​​ρ(⟨v⟩a​e^y​)​​0−10​​⋅​0⟨v⟩a​0​​​rdrdθ=(ρ⟨v⟩a​e^y​)(−⟨v⟩a​)∬rdrdθ=(−ρ⟨v⟩a2​πRa2​)e^y​

Outlet: n^b​=e^vb​​=(−sinθ,−cosθ,0)xyz​; v​b​=⟨v⟩b​(−sinθ,−cosθ,0)xyz​:

∬outlet​ρv​b​(n^⋅v​b​)dS=ρ(⟨v⟩b​e^vb​​)[⟨v⟩b​sin2θ+⟨v⟩b​cos2θ+0]∬rdrdθ=ρ⟨v⟩b2​πRb2​e^vb​​=[ρ⟨v⟩b2​πRb2​]​−sinθ−cosθ0​​xyz​

Overall RTT @ steady state:

on CV∑​F​=∬CS​ρ(v​⋅n^)v​dS=​−ρ⟨v⟩b2​πRb2​sinθ−ρ⟨v⟩a2​πRa2​−ρ⟨v⟩b2​πRb2​cosθ0​​xyz​​

(b) Using macroscopic momentum balance, solve for the overall force on the fluid (@ SS):

on CV∑​F​=dtdP​​​+i=1∑#​[βρAcosθ⟨v⟩2​v^]=βρAcosθ⟨v⟩2​v^​inlet​+βρAcosθ⟨v⟩2​v^​outlet​

(inlet: θa​=180° between n^ and v^; outlet: θb​=0°.)

⇒∑F​=βρπRa2​(−1)⟨v⟩a2​​​010​​+βρπRb2​(1)⟨v⟩b2​​​−sinθ−cosθ0​​;for turbulent flow: β=1 on CV∑​F​=​−ρπRb2​⟨v⟩b2​sinθ−ρπRa2​⟨v⟩a2​−ρπRb2​⟨v⟩b2​cosθ0​​​

(c) Are your force expressions in (a) and (b) different from each other? Why or why not? No! Because RTT & MMB are the one & same → macroscopic look @ CV ↳ using either to arrive at the expression is valid!

Question 2

Consider two concentric disks which are fixed to stay in place. There is an inflow of an incompressible fluid through a hole in the top plate. The flow is driven by a pressure drop, Δp=p(r=aR)−p(r=R), between the inlet at r = aR (a ≪ 1) and the outlet at r = R. (figure: the disks of radius R with the inlet hole of radius aR; front view with plates at z = h and z = −h, flow in from the top and out radially.) The following figure shows the front view of the apparatus above. Consider the cylindrical coordinate system to be positioned in the center.

You can make the following assumptions: (1) the outflow is homogeneous along the circumference; (2) the flow is fully developed and at steady-state; (3) the fluid is incompressible; (4) the outlet is at atmospheric pressure patm​; (5) the effects due to flow around the corner at the inlet can be neglected (a ≪ 1). The pressure at that point is unperturbed by the flow around the corner.

(a) (10 points) Write down the kinematics for this problem by stating physically reasonable assumptions. (i) Which velocity components are non-zero? (ii) Which coordinates (i.e. r, θ, z) do the non-zero velocity component(s) depend on?

Kinematics refer to velocity profiles: (i) v​=(vr​,vθ​,vz​); vθ​=vz​=0; only vr​ is non-zero. (ii) vr​(r,θ​,z) (symmetric).

(b) (20 points) Use the local form of the balance of mass to determine the radial component of the velocity profile in terms of an integration constant.

∇⋅v​=0(@SS, incompressible):r1​∂r∂​(ρrvr​)+r1​∂θ∂​(ρvθ​​)+∂z∂​(ρvz​​)=0⇒∂r∂​(ρrvr​)=0integrate once​vr​=rc1​​​

c1​ has to be a function of z (c1​(z)) (since we know vr​(r,z) & c1​ is a constant w.r.t. variable r).

Transcriber’s note: the intermediate line reads "rvr​=0"; it should be rvr​=c1​.

(c) (50 points) Use the Navier–Stokes equations to find the velocity profile. Start by simplifying them by using your results from (a) and (b). When solving the resulting differential equation, state and apply appropriate boundary conditions. In order to be able to find an analytical solution, neglect the nonlinear term (ρC2/r3, where C is your integration constant from (b)). Express your final answer in terms of Δp, μ, a, R, h, z, r.

(the cylindrical Navier–Stokes equations are pasted beside it with the vanishing terms struck out.)

  • r-direction: ρ(vr​∂r∂vr​​)=−∂r∂P​+μ[∂r∂​(r1​∂r∂​(rvr​))+∂z2∂2vr​​]
  • θ-direction: −r1​∂θ∂P​=0
  • z-direction: −∂z∂P​+ρgz​=0

From part (b): vr​=rc1​(z)​; ∂r∂vr​​=−r2c1​(z)​; ∂r∂​(r⋅vr​)=∂r∂​(r​r​c1​(z)​)=0 (not a function of r!). r-direction:

ρ(rc1​(z)​⋅(−r2c1​(z)​))=−∂r∂P​+μ∂z2∂2​(rc1​(z)​)⇒can neglect as per questionρ(−r3c12​(z)​)​​=−∂r∂P​+rμ​∂z2∂2​(c1​(z))⇒∂r∂P​=rμ​∂z2∂2​(c1​(z))

Transcriber’s note: the term written −∂P/∂r on the right becomes +∂P/∂r in the last line once the nonlinear term is dropped (sign as written).

From the other dimensions: P = f(r, z); −∂z∂P​+ρgz​=0 ⇒ ∂z∂P​=ρgz​ ⇒ P=ρgz​z+c2​(r) ↳ we would need BCs for P in z to solve for c2​(r). BCs for P: @ r = aR, P = P(r = aR) = Pin​; @ r = R, P = P(r = R) = Pout​.

Integrating both sides w.r.t. r:

∫aRR​∂r∂P​dr=∫aRR​rμ​∂z2∂2​(c1​(z))dr⇒P(r,z)​aRR​=μ∂z2∂2​(c1​(z))lnr​aRR​

Δp=P(r=R)−P(r=aR) @ any z:

Δp=μ∂z2∂2​(c1​(z))ln(aRR​)⇒∂z2∂2​c1​(z)=μΔp​⋅(ln(aRR​))−1=λintegrating twice w.r.t. z​c1​(z)=λ2z2​+A1​z+A2​ vr​=rc1​(z)​=2rλz2​+rA1​z​+rA2​​​

Transcriber’s note: the problem statement defines Δp=p(aR)−p(R), the opposite sign of the working’s Δp=P(R)−P(aR); the final sign follows the working.

BCs: @ z = h, vr​=0 ⇒ 0=r1​(2λh2​+A1​h+A2​); @ z = −h, vr​=0 ⇒ 0=r1​(2λh2​+A1​(−h)+A2​). 2 eq; 2 unknowns: 2A2​=−λh2 ⇒ A2​=−2λh2​; A1​=0:

∴vr​(r,z)=r1​(2λz2​−2λh2​)=2rλh2​((hz​)2−1);λ=μΔp​(ln(a1​))−1=−μ(lna)Δp​ vr​(r,z)=2μr(lna)Δph2​(1−(hz​)2)​
